items.text: AMEND AND RECOMMIT TO HIGHER EDUCATION
AMEND AND RECOMMIT TO HIGHER EDUCATION
AMEND BY RESTORING TO ORIGINAL PRINT 5799

items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the education law, in relation to reporting and publishing of
certain financial statements and statistical reports received by the
commissioner of education
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S5799

SPONSOR: THOMAS
 
TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the education law, in relation to
reporting and publishing of certain financial statements and statistical
reports received by the commissioner of education

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:  To protect New Yorkers by increasing
transparency and accountability in the for-profit education industry
through the publication of audited financial statements of for-profit
institutions of higher education.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 amends the education law by adding a new section 239-c to:

- Define the term "for-profit institution of higher education"

- Require a for-profit to file annually with the state department of
education an audited financial statement certified by the owner or oper-
ator of the institution

- Authorize the commissioner to require audited statistical reports upon
a determination that a for-profit institution of higher education has
provided false or inaccurate certified statistical reports

- Require the commissioner to make all annual financial statements and
statistical reports received publicly available on the department's
website

Section 2 amends paragraph e of subdivision 4 of section 5001 of the
education law by adding a new subparagraph (iv) to require the commis-
sioner to make all annual financial statements and statistical reports
received publicly available on the department's website

Section 3 provides the effective date

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Taxpayers invest in the success of New York's students through state-
funded scholarships, some 20 percent of which were accepted at for-pro-
fit institutions in 2015-16. Prospective students, advocacy organiza-
tions, and any interested parties deserve the right to access these
statements as a matter of transparency and to ensure consumers are
empowered in the choices they make.

The rate at which for-profit institutions have been closing their doors
due to financial troubles is cause for concern and a further reason why
the audited financial statements of these schools should be publicly
available for review by consumer protection advocates. The Chronicle of
Higher Education released a report in April 2019 that showed 451,270
students nationwide have been affected by for-profit closures between
2014 and 2018. In New York, 33 for-profit institutions with a total
enrollment of 13,312, closed their doors in the same period of time. The
vast majority of the students at these schools were people of color and
women. Across the country, older and low-income students are dispropor-
tionately affected by this crisis.  School closures are devastating for
students and staff--too often closures happen quickly and without warn-
ing to students who are left without a means to finish their degrees.
Nonprofit colleges in our state are already required to report their
financial information on 990 forms. Financial information for public
institutions is also available. This bill would simply subject for-pro-
fit institutions to a similar standard so New Yorkers know how these
schools spend their tax dollars and have an understanding of the finan-
cial health of these schools.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
Immediately after becoming law.

B.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S5799B

SPONSOR: THOMAS
 
TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the education law, in relation to
reporting and publishing of certain financial statements and statistical
reports received by the commissioner of education

 
PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

To protect New Yorkers by increasing transparency and accountability in
the for-profit education industry through the publication of audited
financial statements of for-profit institutions of higher education.

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 amends the education law by adding a new section 239-c.

- Subdivision 1 defines the term "for-profit institution of higher
education".

- Subdivision 2 states the requirement that the commissioner of educa-
tion must establish a publicly accessible website for the dissemination
of data and disclosures related to for-profit institutions of higher
education. Subparagraphs (a) through (e) state the details of this
requirement.

- Subdivision 3 states rules related to rapid enrollment increases or
decreases at a for profit institution of higher education. Subparagraph
(a) states the requirement that if a program at a for-profit institution
of higher education that has been approved by the department has an
increase in enrollment of fifteen percent or more in any given year, the
department must review the program within thirty business days. Subpara-
graph (b) states the requirement that if a program at a for-profit
institution of higher education that has been approved by the department
has a decrease in enrollment of fifteen percent or more in any given
year, the department must review the program within thirty business
days. Subparagraph (c) outlines restrictive powers of the commissioner
should a violation pursuant to subparagraphs (a) and (b) of this subdi-
vision. Subparagraph (d) states that the commissioner shall promulgate
rules and regulations governing the manner in which enrollment shall be
tracked by the department using existing incoming data. Subparagraph (e)
states that the commissioner's enforcement powers shall not be limited
by this subdivision.

Section 2 states the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

Taxpayers invest in the success of New York's students through state-
funded scholarships, some 20 percent of which were accepted at for-pro-
fit institutions in 2015-16. Prospective students, advocacy organiza-
tions, and any interested parties deserve the right to access these
institution's statements as a matter of transparency and to ensure
consumers are empowered in the choices they make.

The rate at which for-profit institutions have been closing their doors
due to financial troubles is cause for concern and a further reason why
the audited financial statements of these schools should be publicly
available for review by consumer protection advocates. The Chronicle of

students nationwide have been affected by for-profit closures between

tion, the vast majority of the students at these schools were people of
color and women. Across the country, older and low-income students are
disproportionately affected by this crisis. School closures are devas-
tating for students and staff--too often closures happen quickly and
without warning to students who are left without a means to finish their
degrees. Nonprofit colleges in our state are already required to report
their financial information on 990 forms. Financial information for
public institutions is also available. This bill would simply subject
for-profit institutions to a similar standard so New Yorkers know how
these schools spend their tax dollars and have an understanding of the
financial health of these schools.

 
PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New bill.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS FOR STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS:

To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
Immediately after becoming law.

summary: Requires certain for-profit institutions to make annual reports to the commissioner of education and requires the commissioner to make such reports publicly available.
